topics.title: Many Gods, Many Forms
topics.short: Egyptians worshiped many gods; one god could appear in several forms, and several gods could share one role.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptians worshiped animals as animals. Animal heads and forms showed a god's qualities; sacred animals were thought to house the god's presence.

topics.title: Recognizing the Gods
topics.short: Gods are known by their heads, crowns and emblems: Amun's two tall plumes, Osiris's crook and flail, Isis's throne sign, Maat's feather.
topics.trouble: Students identify gods only by animal heads. Several share a head (Ra and Horus are both falcons); the crown or sun disk tells them apart.

topics.title: Gods and Their Cities
topics.short: Each great god had a home city: Ptah at Memphis, Ra at Heliopolis, Amun at Thebes, Thoth at Hermopolis, Osiris at Abydos, Hathor at Dendera.
topics.trouble: Students think every god was worshiped equally everywhere. Each city honored its own gods first.

topics.title: Divine Families
topics.short: Gods were grouped in families of three: Amun, Mut and Khonsu at Thebes; Osiris, Isis and Horus; Ptah, Sekhmet and Nefertem at Memphis.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the triads. Tie each one to its city.

topics.title: The Osiris Myth
topics.short: In the myth, Seth killed his brother Osiris; Isis restored him, and their son Horus won the throne, while Osiris ruled the dead.
topics.trouble: Students expect one fixed version of the story. Egyptian texts give pieces of it; the fullest single telling is by the Greek writer Plutarch.

topics.title: Amun-Ra and Combined Gods
topics.short: Gods could be joined into one, like Amun-Ra, king of the gods in the New Kingdom, joining the hidden Amun and the sun god Ra.
topics.trouble: Students think combined gods replaced the older ones. Amun and Ra were still worshiped separately too.

topics.title: The Heliopolis Account
topics.short: At Heliopolis, Atum rose from the waters of Nun and created Shu and Tefnut, who gave birth to Geb (earth) and Nut (sky): the first gods of the Nine (the Ennead).
topics.trouble: Students list Ra as the first god in every account. At Heliopolis the creator is Atum (later joined with Ra).

topics.title: The Memphis Account
topics.short: At Memphis, Ptah created the world by thought and word; the text survives on the Shabaka Stone (c. 710 BC), and its date of composition is debated.
topics.trouble: Students date the Memphite Theology to the Old Kingdom as fact. The stone is 25th Dynasty; scholars disagree how much older the text is.

topics.title: The Hermopolis Account
topics.short: At Hermopolis, creation began with eight gods (the Ogdoad), four pairs standing for waters, endlessness, darkness and hiddenness.
topics.trouble: Students confuse the Ogdoad (eight, Hermopolis) with the Ennead (nine, Heliopolis).

topics.title: The First Mound
topics.short: The accounts share an image: a mound rising from the waters at the first moment, recalled by the benben stone and by temple floors.
topics.trouble: Students see the accounts as rivals that cancel each other. Egyptians held several side by side.

topics.title: Maat and Isfet
topics.short: Maat was the right order of the world, truth and justice; isfet was disorder. Keeping maat was the duty of gods, kings and people.
topics.trouble: Students think Maat is only a goddess. It is also an idea, the order everyone was to live by.

topics.title: The King Between Gods and People
topics.short: The king was Horus on earth and son of Ra; he stood between the gods and the people, offering to the gods for everyone.
topics.trouble: Students say Egyptians saw the king simply as a god. The office was divine; the man holding it was mortal.

topics.title: The King Offers to the Gods
topics.short: Temple walls show the king offering to the gods in every scene, though priests did the daily work in his name.
topics.trouble: Students think the king performed every ritual in person. Priests acted on his behalf.

topics.title: The Sed Festival
topics.short: The sed festival renewed the king's strength, traditionally after thirty years of rule and then every few years.
topics.trouble: Students think the sed festival was a birthday. It was a jubilee of renewal, usually first held in the 30th year.

topics.title: Cult Temples and Memorial Temples
topics.short: Cult temples housed a god; memorial (mortuary) temples kept up the cult of a dead king, like those on the west bank at Thebes.
topics.trouble: Students think temples were for public worship like churches. Most people never went inside; temples were the gods' houses.

topics.title: The Plan of a Temple
topics.short: From the river: quay, avenue of sphinxes, pylon, open court, hypostyle hall, offering hall and sanctuary.
topics.trouble: Students put the hypostyle hall before the pylon. The pylon is the gateway; everything else lies behind it.

topics.title: The Temple as the World
topics.short: The temple pictured the world at creation: the pylon the horizon, the columns a papyrus marsh, the sanctuary the first mound, rising and darkening inward.
topics.trouble: Students see the plan only as rooms. Each part carried meaning, which is why floors rise and roofs drop toward the sanctuary.

topics.title: The Daily Ritual
topics.short: Each morning priests opened the shrine, woke, washed, dressed and fed the god's statue, then sealed it again.
topics.trouble: Students think the statue was the god. Egyptians believed the god came to dwell in it.

topics.title: Priests
topics.short: Priests served in shifts; ranks included the ḥm-nṯr ("god's servant"), the wꜥb ("pure one") and the lector priest who read the rituals.
topics.trouble: Students picture full-time monks. Many priests served one month in four and then went back to their own lives.

topics.title: Karnak and Luxor
topics.short: Karnak, the temple of Amun at Thebes, grew for two thousand years; an avenue of sphinxes joins it to Luxor Temple.
topics.trouble: Students think Karnak was built at once. Kings from the Middle Kingdom to the Romans added to it.

topics.title: The Opet Festival
topics.short: In the Opet festival, Amun's statue traveled in its sacred boat from Karnak to Luxor Temple, renewing the king's rule.
topics.trouble: Students think festivals were in the temple only. The god's boat was carried out where crowds could see.

topics.title: The Beautiful Festival of the Valley
topics.short: Each year Amun crossed the Nile to the temples of the west bank, and families feasted at the tombs of their dead.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptians avoided cemeteries. Families visited the tombs and shared meals with the dead.

topics.title: Beliefs About the Afterlife
topics.short: Egyptians believed death led to a new life, if the body was kept, the name remembered and offerings continued.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptians were obsessed with death. Their care for the dead came from love of life and the wish to go on living.

topics.title: The Ka, the Ba and the Akh
topics.short: A person had several parts: the ka (life force, which received offerings), the ba (shown as a bird with a human head, free to move), the akh (the transfigured spirit), the name and the shadow.
topics.trouble: Students equate the ba with the soul in later religions. Egyptian ideas divide the person differently; avoid one-word equivalents.

topics.title: The Judgment of the Dead
topics.short: The heart was weighed against the feather of Maat before Osiris; the dead declared they had not done wrongs, and a monster waited for those who failed.
topics.trouble: Students think the heart had to be heavy. It had to balance the feather: free of wrongdoing.

topics.title: The Duat and the Sun's Night Journey
topics.short: The Duat was the realm of the dead, through which the sun god sailed each night to be reborn at dawn.
topics.trouble: Students picture the Duat as an underground hell. It was a realm of passage and renewal, as well as danger.

topics.title: The Field of Reeds
topics.short: The blessed dead hoped to live in the Field of Reeds, a perfect Egypt where crops grew tall; shabti figures would do their work.
topics.trouble: Students think shabtis were toys or portraits. They were helpers meant to answer when the dead were called to work.

topics.title: Offerings for the Dead
topics.short: Families and priests brought food and drink to a tomb's false door and said the offering formula, so the dead would be fed.
topics.trouble: Students think the false door was a fake. It was the meeting place between the living and the dead.

topics.title: Why Mummify?
topics.short: Egyptians preserved the body so the ka and ba could return to it; dry desert graves had first shown them that bodies could last.
topics.trouble: Students think all Egyptians were mummified. Full mummification was costly; many people had simpler burials.

topics.title: How Bodies Were Preserved
topics.short: Embalmers removed the internal organs, dried the body with natron salt for about forty days, then wrapped it in linen with amulets; the whole process took about seventy days.
topics.trouble: Students think the brain was kept with care. Embalmers did not keep it; the heart was usually left in place.

topics.title: Coffins, Canopic Jars and Masks
topics.short: Organs went into four canopic jars guarded by the Four Sons of Horus; the body lay in nested coffins, sometimes with a mask over the face.
topics.trouble: Students mix up the canopic jars' lids. The Four Sons of Horus have human, baboon, jackal and falcon heads.

topics.title: The Pyramid Texts
topics.short: The oldest religious texts, spells carved inside pyramids from Unas (end of the 5th Dynasty) on, to help the king rise to the sky.
topics.trouble: Students think the Great Pyramid has texts inside. The Pyramid Texts start about two centuries later, with Unas.

topics.title: The Coffin Texts
topics.short: In the Middle Kingdom, spells were painted inside the coffins of officials, so non-royal people could use them too.
topics.trouble: Students think only kings had afterlife texts in all periods. By the Middle Kingdom, officials did too.

topics.title: The Book of the Dead
topics.short: From the New Kingdom, spells for the journey through the afterlife were written on papyrus rolls placed in the tomb; Egyptians called them "spells for going forth by day".
topics.trouble: Students think the Book of the Dead was one fixed book. Each roll was a selection of spells, made for its owner.

topics.title: Books of the Underworld
topics.short: New Kingdom royal tombs show the sun's night journey hour by hour, in books like the Amduat ("What Is in the Underworld").
topics.trouble: Students confuse the Amduat (royal tombs, the sun's journey) with the Book of the Dead (papyri for many people).

topics.title: Mastaba Tombs
topics.short: Early elite tombs were mastabas: low, flat-topped buildings over a burial shaft, with a chapel for offerings.
topics.trouble: Students think pyramids came first. Mastabas came first, and the first pyramid began as a mastaba.

topics.title: The Pyramid Complex
topics.short: A pyramid stood in a complex: a valley temple by the river, a covered causeway, and a mortuary temple against the pyramid.
topics.trouble: Students picture pyramids standing alone in the sand. Each was the center of temples and smaller pyramids.

topics.title: Rock-Cut Tombs
topics.short: From the Middle Kingdom, many tombs were cut into cliffs, as at Beni Hasan; New Kingdom kings were buried in the Valley of the Kings.
topics.trouble: Students think pyramids were given up because they were too hard to build. Theft and changing beliefs both played a part; the reasons are debated.

topics.title: Why Tombs Were Decorated
topics.short: Scenes of farming, feasting and offering were meant to provide for the dead forever, not only to record their lives.
topics.trouble: Students read tomb scenes as snapshots of real events. They show an ideal life for eternity.

topics.title: Composite Views
topics.short: Artists drew each part from its most typical view: the face in profile, the eye from the front, shoulders from the front, legs in profile.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptians could not draw perspective. They chose to show each part clearly, as they knew it to be.

topics.title: The Grid and the Canon of Proportions
topics.short: Artists drew figures on a grid: a standing figure was 18 squares from the soles to the hairline, and a later grid used 21 squares.
topics.trouble: Students think the grid was invented by modern scholars. Grids survive on unfinished walls.

topics.title: Size Shows Importance
topics.short: The most important figure is the largest: the king larger than his enemies, a tomb owner larger than his servants.
topics.trouble: Students read size as height or distance. In Egyptian art, size shows rank.

topics.title: Colors and Their Meanings
topics.short: Colors carried meaning: black for fertile soil and rebirth, green for growth, red for energy or danger, gold for the flesh of the gods.
topics.trouble: Students think black skin on Osiris shows his origin. Black and green showed rebirth.

topics.title: Registers and Ground Lines
topics.short: Scenes run in horizontal bands (registers), each with its own ground line; figures face the way the text runs.
topics.trouble: Students read registers as a single scene in depth. Each band is its own row, read like lines of text.

topics.title: Kinds of Statues
topics.short: Common types are the seated statue, the standing striding statue (left foot forward), the scribe statue, the block statue and the pair statue.
topics.trouble: Students think the forward left foot shows walking. It is a convention of standing statues of men.

topics.title: Raised and Sunk Relief
topics.short: Raised relief cuts away the background; sunk relief cuts the figure into the wall and suits bright sun outdoors.
topics.trouble: Students confuse the two. In sunk relief, the edges of the figure go into the stone.

topics.title: Painting and Pigments
topics.short: Painters used mineral colors, including the first known synthetic pigment, Egyptian blue, on plaster or stone.
topics.trouble: Students think Egyptian art was the plain stone color we see today. Most was painted in bright colors.

topics.title: The Art of the Amarna Age
topics.short: Under Akhenaten, art changed: long faces, rounded bodies, family scenes, and the Aten's rays ending in hands.
topics.trouble: Students take Amarna portraits as medical evidence of illness. They reflect a new artistic style; what it meant is debated.

topics.title: Household Gods
topics.short: At home, people turned to protectors like Bes and Taweret, especially for childbirth and children.
topics.trouble: Students think only temple gods mattered. Daily life had its own gods.

topics.title: Amulets
topics.short: People wore amulets for protection: the wedjat eye, the scarab, the ankh, the djed pillar and the tyet knot.
topics.trouble: Students think amulets were only jewelry. They were worn for protection, in life and in the tomb.

topics.title: Oracles and Letters to the Dead
topics.short: People asked gods questions through oracles at festivals and wrote letters to dead relatives asking for help.
topics.trouble: Students think ordinary people had no way to reach the gods. Oracles and letters show how they did.
